questions.prompt: Which statement is the most accurate definition of a distributed system, as Lesson 1 defines it?
options: A collection of independent computers, each with its own memory and clock, that coordinate with each other over a network so that, to users and programs, they appear as a single coherent system
A single powerful computer with multiple CPU cores running many threads in parallel
Any application that stores its data in the cloud rather than on a local hard drive
A set of computers that share memory and a synchronized clock to run one program together
A backup server that only becomes active once the primary machine fails
A group of microservices that must all run on the same physical machine to keep latency low
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines a distributed system as independent computers — each with its own memory, its own clock, and its own chance of failing separately — that coordinate over a network to look like one coherent system to the people and programs using it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D is the closest wrong answer because it also describes 'a set of computers,' but it gets the defining fact backwards: the lesson is explicit that nothing is shared except the network. A distributed system has no shared memory and no global clock — that absence is exactly what makes it hard, not a feature it has.

questions.prompt: A system's SLA promises 99.99% availability ("four nines"). Per Lesson 2's table, roughly how much downtime per year does that actually allow?
options: About 52.6 minutes
About 8.76 hours
About 5.26 minutes
About 3.65 days
questions.explain: Lesson 2's table lists 99.99% ("four nines") as about 52.6 minutes of allowed downtime per year — roughly a tenth of three nines' 8.76 hours, consistent with each additional nine cutting allowed downtime by about a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 3, a load balancer with no redundant backup of its own becomes a ________ for the entire fleet of servers sitting behind it.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 points out that a load balancer is exactly the kind of component that needs its own redundancy, since an unreplicated load balancer becomes a single point of failure (SPOF) for every server behind it, no matter how many of those servers there are.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about vertical versus horizontal scaling, per Lesson 3.
options: Vertical scaling adds more resources (CPU, RAM) to the single machine you already have, and has a hard ceiling once you're on the largest machine a provider sells
Horizontal scaling adds more machines to share the load instead of enlarging one, and doesn't hit the same ceiling vertical scaling does
Horizontal scaling removes the need for a load balancer entirely, since any machine can now answer any request directly
Sharding splits a dataset across multiple machines by a shard key, which is what lets horizontal scaling apply to stateful systems, not just stateless ones
Vertical scaling improves fault isolation, because a single bigger machine is less likely to fail than several smaller ones
questions.explain: Vertical scaling enlarges one machine and hits a hard ceiling; horizontal scaling adds machines and avoids that ceiling; sharding is how horizontal scaling extends to stateful data. Horizontal scaling only works because a load balancer spreads requests across the pool — without one you'd just have idle and overloaded machines. Vertical scaling keeps the single point of failure exactly where it was, since one bigger machine is still one machine; it does not improve fault isolation.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 2 and 4 to what it actually means.
right: A system keeps working correctly over a stretch of time, including when parts of it fail
The fraction of time a system is usable out of the total time it's supposed to be running
Losing some functionality during a failure instead of losing all of it
Running more than one copy of a critical component so one failing doesn't take everything down
questions.explain: Availability is the fraction of time a system is usable, a snapshot measure. Reliability is whether a system keeps working correctly over time, including under failure. Redundancy means running more than one copy of something critical. Graceful degradation means a failure costs you some functionality, not all of it.

questions.prompt: Order these SLA availability levels from Lesson 2, from the most downtime allowed per year to the least.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 walks through these four SLA levels in exactly this order, noting that each additional nine cuts the allowed downtime by roughly a factor of ten — from days, to hours, to under an hour, to a few minutes.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly captures what the CAP theorem actually proves, per Lesson 8?
options: When a network partition actually occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot provide both at the same time
A distributed system can only ever implement two of the three properties — consistency, availability, partition tolerance — and must permanently pick which two to support
Partition tolerance is an optional feature that a well-designed system can simply choose to skip
Consistency and availability can both always be guaranteed simultaneously, regardless of whether a partition occurs
The CAP theorem says a system must choose between latency and consistency at all times, partition or not
The CAP theorem applies only to relational databases, not to distributed systems in general
questions.explain: The precise statement, proven by Gilbert and Lynch, is that a network partition forces a choice between consistency and availability at that moment — a replica that can't reach the rest of the cluster must either refuse to answer (consistency) or answer anyway with possibly stale data (availability). Outside of an actual partition, a system can usually offer both just fine.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the popular 'pick any two of three' simplification the lesson explicitly calls misleading. It treats partition tolerance as optional, like consistency and availability — but in any real multi-machine system, network partitions will eventually happen regardless of what you'd prefer, so it isn't a feature you opt out of. The real, forced choice is only between C and A, and only once a partition actually occurs.

questions.prompt: A node sends a message to another node and receives no response at all. Per Lesson 6, what can it actually conclude about the other node's state?
options: Nothing with certainty — the silence could equally mean the node is slow, the message was dropped, the response was lost in transit, or the node has crashed
The node has definitely crashed, since a healthy node would always respond before any timeout
The message definitely wasn't delivered, since asynchronous systems guarantee a response within a fixed window
The node is definitely just slow and never actually dead, since networks always eventually deliver every message
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that a slow node, a dropped request, a lost response, and a dead node all look identical from the sender's side: silence. Every failure-detection mechanism covered later is really just a policy for guessing when enough silence means 'probably dead,' because the system can never know for certain.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 6 describes Lamport's concept of ________ ordering, which lets a distributed system reason about which of two events occurred first using causality, instead of relying on wall-clock time.
questions.explain: Happens-before ordering says event A happens-before event B if A could have influenced B, such as 'send a message' before 'receive that message.' Two events with no such causal link are concurrent, and no meaningful ordering exists between them at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about BASE and eventual consistency, per Lesson 7.
options: Basically Available means the system responds to requests most of the time, even during partial failures
Soft state means the data may change over time even without new input, as replicas converge
BASE guarantees every read reflects the most recent write everywhere, exactly the same as strong consistency
Eventual consistency means that, given enough time with no new writes, all replicas eventually agree on the same value
BASE is simply ACID implemented badly — an inferior fallback rather than a deliberate design trade-off
questions.explain: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency, and all three descriptions here are accurate. BASE is explicitly not the same guarantee as strong consistency — it deliberately relaxes 'every read sees the latest write' in exchange for availability and lower latency — and the lesson is explicit that this is a deliberate trade, not ACID done poorly.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 7 and 8 to its correct description.
right: Every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data anywhere
Attach a timestamp to each write and keep whichever one is newest
Data structures designed so concurrent updates can always be merged automatically, without losing information
Each replica tracks a per-replica counter so the system can tell whether one write happened-before another, or whether they were truly concurrent
questions.explain: Last-write-wins keeps whichever write has the newest timestamp. Version vectors let replicas detect happened-before ordering versus true concurrency. CRDTs are built so concurrent updates merge automatically with no lost information. Strong consistency is the stricter guarantee that every read reflects the single most recent write everywhere.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Raft-style leader election, from Lesson 10, in the order they actually occur after a leader fails.
items: Followers expect regular heartbeats from the leader
A follower's election timer expires with no heartbeat, and it suspects the leader has failed
That follower becomes a candidate, increments a term number, and requests votes from the other nodes
Each node votes for at most one candidate per term
A candidate that receives votes from a majority of the cluster becomes the new leader for that term
questions.explain: Followers normally rely on the leader's heartbeats; a missed heartbeat past the election timeout makes a follower suspect failure and become a candidate requesting votes under a new term; each node casts at most one vote per term; and only a candidate who wins a majority becomes the new leader — the majority requirement is what guarantees at most one leader per term.

questions.prompt: A client sends a non-idempotent "add $100 to my account balance" request, gets no response, and retries the exact same request once more. Per Lesson 11, if the first attempt had actually succeeded, what happens?
options: The balance increases by $200 total, because "add $100" is not idempotent — each successful execution adds another $100
The balance increases by only $100 total, because all retries are inherently safe regardless of the operation
The second request is automatically rejected, because servers always detect duplicate requests without any extra mechanism
The balance decreases, because a retry following a lost response is treated as a cancellation of the first attempt
questions.explain: "Add $100" is explicitly the lesson's example of a non-idempotent operation: running it twice adds $200, not $100. Since the caller can't tell whether its first request succeeded and only the response was lost, retrying without an idempotency key risks exactly this double-execution — which is the whole reason idempotency keys exist.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 12, Salesforce's governor limits are best understood as a real-world expression of which distributed-systems concept from earlier in the course?
options: Rate limiting — a deliberate cap on usage enforced regardless of how much a given transaction needs
Eventual consistency — governor limits let data converge slowly across different orgs
Leader election — governor limits decide which org's transaction is allowed to run first
Distributed tracing — governor limits record a transaction's path as it crosses multiple services
questions.explain: Lesson 12 frames governor limits as exactly the rate-limiting idea from earlier in the course: a cap on SOQL queries, CPU time, DML statements, and callouts that applies regardless of what a transaction wants, protecting the shared multi-tenant platform from any one tenant's runaway usage.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce's asynchronous tooling, per Lesson 12.
options: Platform Events implement a publish/subscribe pattern, letting one published event be consumed independently by multiple subscribers
Batch Apex processes large volumes of records in chunks over multiple asynchronous transactions
Change Data Capture requires external systems to continuously poll Salesforce in order to detect record changes
Future methods and Queueable Apex let a transaction hand work off to run later, instead of making the user wait inside the same request
Governor limits and Platform Events are machinery unique to Salesforce, with no equivalent concept anywhere else in distributed systems
questions.explain: Platform Events are Salesforce's pub/sub mechanism; Batch Apex chunks large jobs across multiple asynchronous transactions; Future methods and Queueable Apex move work off the synchronous request path. Change Data Capture publishes change events automatically so external systems react to them, rather than needing to poll. And the lesson's whole point is that none of this is Salesforce-specific — it's the same handful of distributed-systems ideas expressed in Salesforce's vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 13, the ________ pattern — named after a ship's watertight compartments — isolates resources like thread pools so that one failing dependency can't exhaust resources shared by everything else.
questions.explain: The bulkhead pattern confines resources used to call a given dependency to their own limited pool, so that dependency failing and filling up its pool only blocks requests that actually need it — unrelated requests to other dependencies keep flowing normally.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 14 to its correct description.
right: A deliberate cap on request rate set in advance, enforced regardless of whether the system is busy right now
A bucket refilled at a steady rate; each request consumes one token, which naturally allows short bursts
A system signaling upstream, based on its current condition, that it cannot keep up and the sender should slow down
Requests fill a bucket that leaks (processes requests) at a constant rate regardless of how fast it's filling, producing a strictly smooth output
questions.explain: Backpressure is a dynamic, reactive signal based on current load. Rate limiting is a predetermined ceiling applied whether the system is busy or idle. Token bucket allows bursts up to an accumulated balance. Leaky bucket enforces a strictly constant processing rate with no bursting.

questions.prompt: A team has an alert that fires whenever error rate crosses a known 5% threshold — how they first learn something is wrong. Diagnosing the actual root cause, though, requires digging through logs and traces for a pattern nobody wrote an alert for. Per Lesson 15, which best distinguishes these two activities?
options: The alert is monitoring — watching a known metric against a known threshold; the investigation is observability — the ability to ask new, unanticipated questions using already-collected data
The alert is observability and the investigation is monitoring — the two labels are simply reversed
Both activities are examples of monitoring, since both ultimately rely on metrics the team configured in advance
Both activities are examples of observability, since both involve examining system data after something went wrong
questions.explain: Lesson 15 draws this exact line: monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance, like a fixed error-rate threshold. Observability is the broader property of being able to investigate a question nobody anticipated — like why only one customer's requests on one code path are slow — using the logs, metrics, and traces already being collected.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Lesson 16 checkout case study in the order they actually occur.
items: The load balancer routes the incoming checkout request to one of several identical service instances
The service checks inventory, a value treated as eventually consistent (AP) since a few seconds of staleness is an acceptable risk
The service charges the customer's card, a strongly consistent (CP) operation, attaching an idempotency key before the call
The service publishes an "order placed" message to a queue and returns success to the customer immediately
The fulfillment system consumes the queued message whenever it's ready, decoupled from the original checkout request
questions.explain: The case study's checkout flow runs in exactly this order: route the request, check inventory under an AP trade-off, charge the card under a CP trade-off with an idempotency key in case of a timeout-triggered retry, publish to a queue and return success immediately, and let fulfillment consume the message on its own schedule afterward.

questions.prompt: Three nodes in a cluster lose network contact with the other two for 30 seconds, then reconnect. Per Lesson 17's third practice scenario, could both the three isolated nodes and the two remaining nodes keep accepting writes to the same data during that window?
options: Only if the system accepts an availability-favoring (AP) choice, and has a conflict-resolution strategy like last-write-wins or a CRDT ready to reconcile the two sides afterward
Yes, always — partition tolerance by itself guarantees both sides can keep accepting writes safely, with no further reconciliation needed
No — a network partition always means the entire cluster, on both sides, stops accepting writes until the partition heals
Only the side with a majority of nodes can ever accept writes; the minority side always rejects every request outright, in every system
questions.explain: This is the practice lesson's own answer: both sides accepting writes during the split is only possible under an AP choice, and even then the system needs a conflict-resolution strategy like last-write-wins or a CRDT to reconcile conflicting writes once the partition heals. A CP system would instead refuse writes on the minority side (or both sides) until it heals.
